title: Design exercise: search autocomplete
summary: A classic design exercise: search-box suggestions within a 100 ms budget at tens of thousands of requests per second. The reference answer precomputes the top ten completions per prefix from an hourly, decayed aggregation of the query log, serves them from in-memory shards by first letters behind a short-TTL edge cache, re-ranks with the user's own recent queries, and treats freshness as a cost dial on the build pipeline.

exercise.prompt: Design the search box suggestions for a large consumer site: as the user types, show the ten most likely completions within the time it takes to type the next character. Suggestions should reflect what people are searching for now, not last year.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Return the top 10 completions for a prefix of 1 to 20 characters; rank by popularity with recency; exclude blocked terms.
Optionally re-rank by the user's own recent queries; update suggestions from the query log within an hour.
100 million searches per day; each search session sends about 5 prefix requests, so 500 million autocomplete requests per day.
Peak 10 times the daily average; a vocabulary of the top 10 million distinct queries worth suggesting.
derive the request rate, the index size and the memory per shard yourself
p99 under 100 ms end to end at the client, which leaves about 20 ms inside the service after network time (assumption).
99.9 percent availability; the box must never block search itself.
Full search, spell correction beyond a fallback, query understanding, ads in suggestions.

clarifying_questions.q: Are suggestions whole queries or next words?
clarifying_questions.a: Whole queries that start with the prefix; mid-word matches are out of scope.
A query trending now should appear within an hour; a query that stopped being popular should fade over days, not vanish at once.
Lightly: the user's own recent queries are boosted among the global candidates; no per-user index.
Case-folded; one language per site locale, each with its own index; typo tolerance only as a fallback when the prefix has no completions.

clarifying_questions.q: Is exactness of popularity counts needed?
clarifying_questions.a: No; approximate counts with hourly refresh are fine.
Blocked terms (a curated list), personal data that appears in queries, and anything seen fewer than a minimum number of times (assumption: 10 in the window).

blocks.text: Two halves. Serving: an edge cache keyed by prefix (the same prefixes repeat constantly, so a short TTL cache absorbs most traffic), an autocomplete service that reads a precomputed top-10 list for the prefix from an in-memory shard and optionally re-ranks it with the user's recent queries. Build: an hourly aggregation of the query log into decayed counts, filtering, and a versioned rebuild of the per-prefix top-10 lists that shards load atomically. The serving side never computes popularity; it only looks up.

blocks.text: The edge cache works because the response carries Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, which RFC 9111 defines as the directive that lets shared caches and browsers reuse the response for that long; a blocked term can therefore linger for up to a minute unless its prefix keys are purged, which the failure table covers.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: One keystroke, and one hourly build.

blocks.title: Debounce, look up, re-rank, fall back, rebuild
items: The client waits 100 ms after the keystroke, then requests the prefix; the edge cache answers if it has seen the prefix within 60 s (for the top few thousand prefixes this is nearly always).
On a miss, the service hashes the prefix's first characters to a shard, reads the PrefixEntry from the shard's in-memory map (replicas chosen round robin), and gets up to 10 query ids with scores.
If the user is known, the service merges the user's recent queries that start with the prefix, boosting them ahead of global results; it never shows another user's queries.

If the prefix has no entry (a rare or misspelled prefix), the service falls back to a term or phrase suggester over the query vocabulary for a correction, bounded by a 10 ms deadline, else returns an empty list.

Build, every hour: the aggregator reads the last hour of the query log, adds counts to a decayed score (yesterday's count weighs half, assumption), drops queries below the minimum count or on the block list, recomputes the top 10 for every affected prefix, writes a new index version to object storage, and tells shards to load it. Shards load the new version beside the old and switch pointers, so no request sees a partial index.

blocks.text: The serving path is a cache in front of a memory lookup; it scales by replicas, and its only risk is a cold start after a deploy, which is why shards load the index from a prebuilt file rather than computing it. The real bottleneck is the build: recomputing top-10 for 100 million prefixes every hour is a batch job over the query log, parallel by prefix range, and its runtime bounds freshness.

blocks.text: Hot shards (common first letters) get more replicas than cold ones, assigned from measured traffic per shard rather than evenly; the edge cache already removes most of the skew because popular prefixes are exactly the cached ones. Discord's message search write-up is the reference for the opposite shape, sharding a search index by owning entity and indexing lazily on first use; it does not fit here because autocomplete has one global vocabulary per locale, but the lesson that index layout follows the query pattern does.
Each row names the failure, what the user sees, and the mitigation.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: whole-query completions, freshness within an hour, light personalisation, case folding and locales, what must never be suggested. Say the numbers aloud: 58,000 requests per second at peak after debouncing, 100 million prefixes, about 10 GB of index, a 20 ms service budget inside a 100 ms client target.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Query with a decayed score, PrefixEntry with a top-10 list, UserRecent, IndexVersion; the suggest endpoint with public caching headers.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: the serving half (edge cache, service, in-memory shards, re-rank) and the build half (log, aggregator, filter, versioned builder). Name the three index structures and why precomputed lists make the choice unimportant.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: the build pipeline (decay, minimum counts, block list, atomic version swap, freshness bound), then serving under skew (sharding by first letters, replicas by traffic, the edge cache removing the hot prefixes, the fallback deadline).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (regional index files, incremental builds, trending lane, abuse controls), and the L3 sentence: the serving path is trivial on purpose; the design is the build pipeline and its freshness-versus-cost dial.
Context and scope: The search product, the existing query log and its retention, the locales served, and the latency complaints or stale suggestions that motivate the work.
Goals and non-goals: Top-10 completions under 100 ms at p99, freshness within an hour, light personalisation; no full search, no spell correction beyond a fallback, no ads.
Design: This answer fills it: the serving path, the index layout, the hourly build with versioned swap, the fallback.
Alternatives considered: Ranking at request time, trie versus sorted sets versus FST suggester, prefix-hash sharding, a per-user index, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Privacy (no personal data in suggestions, per-user recents with a TTL and never shared), abuse (block list ownership, log rate limits), observability (edge hit ratio, index age, empty-result rate, fallback rate), cost (memory per replica, build compute per hour), rollout by locale with the index version pinned.
Review questions the doc must answer: How a blocked term is removed from every cache within minutes, and what the service returns when the index is older than its freshness target.
